Chairperson, the Russian Federation's Global Navigation Satellite System, GLONASS, provides coordinate time and navigation support basic services that allow any user with the requisite equipment and located at any point on the earth's surface to determine their position and the time with guaranteed parameters. The services provided by two navigation signals available on open access with frequency division in the L1 and L2 radio frequency bands transmitted by all GLONASS system satellites that comprise the constellation of the present time. The second satellite, GLONASS-K2, of the new generation GLONASS system was successfully placed in orbit in March 2025. This is a major step forward for GLONASS. This satellite transmits three open access signals with code division in radio frequency bands L1, L2, and L3. GLONASS system open access signals with code division are more powerful and feature enhanced signal to noise ratios compared to GLONASS system open access signals with frequency division. They're also more resilient to multipath effects. Additionally, they incorporate a global ionospheric model to compensate for anticipated ionospheric delay. This makes the signals highly noise immune and enhances the accuracy of user positioning services, including in highly urbanized environments. The GLONASS-K2 satellite will be used to increase testing of the signals for civilian uses worldwide. We plan that by 2036, 24 GLONASS satellites will be transmitting these signals, allowing us to operationalize them and thus enhance the characteristics and quality of the coordinate time and navigational basic services provided by GLONASS system, or rather to GLONASS system users. We are strongly committed to a consistent policy of the free of charge provision of coordinate time and navigational basic services. and GLONASS system open access signals without any restrictions whatsoever and without deliberately downgrading characteristics. We firmly believe that our policy will support equal access to space technologies in today's world, uninterrupted user access to global navigation satellite system open access signals is essential to economic growth across many sectors of the global economy. as well as social progress and achieving the SDGs, the Russian Federation is committed to the continued development of the GLONASS system for the benefit of civilian users worldwide. The satellites provide ongoing monitoring of blind zones, particularly in the Arctic. When signals are received, they are transmitted to terrestrial systems. And they're used in rescue services. Of particular note is the establishment of the Global Ionized Observation Operation Network, GEOM, operating under the ISWCF framework. GEOM serves as a comprehensive global representative body for ionized operators and users. The current financially constrained situation of WMO has impacted the space weather activities within the WMO Secretariat. At the WMO Extraordinary Congress, EC, held in October 2025, member states decided the implementation of space weather activities would anyway continue within existing resources.
